Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The self-blame item is not clinically supported elsewhere in the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal or Memory items indicating guilt, responsibility, shame, or a trauma narrative that would make repeated self-blame coherent. With this formulation, the only strong cycle is Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly function to manage current danger/safety concerns. Drug use and avoiding thinking fit that threat-management loop, but repeated self-blame instead implies an unrepresented negative-appraisal process and sits weakly with the rest of the selected items.

vignette: The incident began with a routine traffic stop that unraveled in seconds. Minh had barely pulled over when two officers approached, their voices sharp and impatient. When he fumbled for his registration, one officer stepped forward, shoved him against the hood, and pinned his wrists until his shoulders burned. The humiliation of being forced into submission, the sudden violence, and the chilling certainty that his compliance had only delayed the next blow fractured his sense of security. In the months that followed, the memory did not fade; it sharpened. At his family's carpentry shop, waiting for a delivery of lumber or watching a customer hesitate before speaking triggered a physical alarm that tightened his chest. He stopped trusting open doorways, instinctively positioning himself with his back pressed to the nearest structural wall, his eyes constantly sweeping the floorboards for any movement that might signal another confrontation. Even when he finally returned home, his muscles refused to uncoil. He lay awake, fully alert, convinced that the next wrong move would bring the same sudden pressure. The unrelenting sense of imminent danger pulled him into a narrow corridor of coping. Because his nervous system remained locked in alarm, he found himself drowning in replayed fragments of the encounter, dissecting every second to find where he might have submitted sooner. He told himself that if he had just moved faster, the officer might have let him walk away. This relentless self-reproach became a heavy anchor, driving him to seek relief in the only thing that temporarily quieted the static. He began taking leftover sedatives after evening shifts, downing them with whiskey until his thoughts finally blurred. When the memories grew too vivid, he deliberately forced himself to focus on the grain of the oak planks he was planing, pushing the image of the cruiser from his mind. Each attempt to dull the fear, however, only left the underlying tension untouched. The very habits he built to survive the initial shock now fed the alarm that never slept. Every time he swallowed a pill or diverted his eyes from a memory, the unprocessed dread pooled in his gut, resurfacing stronger the next time a work order was delayed or a client questioned a cut. He stopped discussing the past with Clara, which created a quiet distance between them, but the real cost was in the workshop. His inability to settle into a rhythm meant his hands grew stiff, his measurements faltered, and the foreman began questioning his reliability. The more he avoided the truth of what had happened, the more the environment itself felt like a trap. The sedatives and the forced mental distance did not drain the threat; they starved his mind of the chance to recalibrate, leaving him perpetually braced for the next blow. The cycle tightened relentlessly: the dread demanded escape, the escape deepened the dread, and the workshop, once his sanctuary, now felt like a trap he was waiting to flee. After two years of carrying that weight, Minh finally walked into a clinic when Clara discovered the empty bottles and quietly placed an appointment card on the kitchen counter. He no longer trusts his own stillness, and the exhaustion of perpetually scanning for danger has made even simple conversations feel like negotiations. He hopes to find a way to sleep without his spine pressed against the wall, to let a delayed delivery pass without his pulse hammering, and to finally stop punishing himself for a moment he cannot rewrite. What he fears most is that he has spent so long preparing for an ambush that he no longer knows how to simply exist.
